name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q35 - Kinetic and stereochemical features of bimolecular substitution

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements correctly summarizes the kinetic and stereochemical features of an \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) nucleophilic substitution reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Kinetic Order of \(\mathrm{S_N2}\)
The rate of an \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) reaction depends on the concentration of both the substrate (alkyl halide) and the attacking nucleophile: \(\mathrm{Rate = k[RX][Nu^-]}\), establishing second-order kinetics.

Step 2: Mechanism and Transition State
The reaction takes place in a single concerted step without any discrete intermediate. The incoming nucleophile forms a bond simultaneously as the leaving group departs, passing through a pentacoordinated transition state where carbon is partially bonded to five atoms.

Step 3: Stereochemical Outcome
Because the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite to the departing leaving group, the spatial configuration of the carbon atom inverts (Walden inversion, analogous to an umbrella turning inside out).

Step 4: Conclusion
The \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) reaction follows second-order kinetics, occurs in a single concerted step, and gives complete inversion of configuration.

Final Answer:
It follows second-order kinetics, occurs in a single concerted step through a pentacoordinated transition state, and proceeds with complete inversion of configuration

answer.text: It follows first-order kinetics, occurs in two steps via a carbocation intermediate, and proceeds with racemisation
It follows second-order kinetics, occurs in two steps via a carbanion intermediate, and proceeds with retention of configuration
It follows second-order kinetics, occurs in a single concerted step through a pentacoordinated transition state, and proceeds with complete inversion of configuration
It follows first-order kinetics, occurs in a single concerted step, and proceeds with complete retention of configuration

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q36 - Steric factors governing bimolecular substitution rates

questiontext.text: What is the correct sequence of relative reactivity of alkyl halides towards \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) substitution reactions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mechanism Requirement for \(\mathrm{S_N2}\)
\(\mathrm{S_N2}\) substitution requires backside attack of the incoming nucleophile on the carbon bearing the leaving group.

Step 2: Role of Steric Hindrance
Bulky alkyl substituents on or adjacent to the electrophilic carbon atom exert severe steric hindrance, physically blocking the approach of the nucleophile to the reactive carbon.

Step 3: Relative Rate Comparison
Methyl halides have only small hydrogen atoms and react most rapidly (relative rate \(\approx 30\)). Primary halides have one alkyl group (relative rate \(\approx 1\)), secondary halides have two (relative rate \(\approx 0.02\)), and tertiary halides have three bulky alkyl groups that completely block backside attack (relative rate \(\approx 0\)).

Step 4: Conclusion
The reactivity order towards \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) is methyl > primary > secondary > tertiary.

Final Answer:
\(\mathrm{CH_3X > 1^\circ\text{ alkyl halide} > 2^\circ\text{ alkyl halide} > 3^\circ\text{ alkyl halide}}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q37 - Mechanism and solvent effect in unimolecular substitution

questiontext.text: An \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction between tert-butyl bromide and hydroxide ion follows first-order kinetics primarily because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Kinetic Law of \(\mathrm{S_N1}\)
The rate of an \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction depends exclusively on the concentration of the alkyl halide: \(\mathrm{Rate = k[(CH_3)_3CBr]}\).

Step 2: Two-Step Reaction Mechanism
Step I is the slow heterolysis of the polarised \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond to form a planar carbocation intermediate and a bromide ion: \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3CBr \xrightarrow{slow} (CH_3)_3C^+ + Br^-}\). Step II is the rapid attack of the nucleophile (\(\mathrm{OH^-}\)) on the carbocation to form the alcohol.

Step 3: Rate Determining Step Analysis
The overall rate is governed by the slowest step (Step I), which involves solely the alkyl halide and does not depend on the nucleophile concentration.

Step 4: Conclusion
The reaction is first-order because the rate-determining step is the unimolecular ionisation of the carbon-bromine bond.

Final Answer:
The rate-determining slow step involves only the unimolecular cleavage of the carbon-bromine bond to produce a carbocation intermediate

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q38 - Resonance stabilization of intermediate carbocations

questiontext.text: Why do allylic and benzylic halides exhibit exceptionally high reactivity towards \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) nucleophilic substitution reactions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Determinant of \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) Reactivity
The rate of an \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction is directly governed by the ease of formation and thermodynamic stability of the intermediate carbocation.

Step 2: Allylic Carbocation Resonance
In allylic halides, heterolysis yields the allyl carbocation (\(\mathrm{CH_2=CH-\overset{+}{C}H_2 \longleftrightarrow \overset{+}{C}H_2-CH=CH_2}\)), where the positive charge is delocalised across two carbons through the adjacent pi system.

Step 3: Benzylic Carbocation Resonance
In benzylic halides, the benzyl carbocation (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-\overset{+}{C}H_2}\)) is stabilised by delocalisation of the positive charge throughout the aromatic ring across four canonical resonating structures.

Step 4: Conclusion
Allylic and benzylic halides react rapidly in \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) because their carbocations are stabilized through resonance.

Final Answer:
The carbocations formed in the rate-determining slow step are greatly stabilised by resonance delocalisation

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q39 - Leaving group ability of halide ions

questiontext.text: For a given alkyl group (\(\mathrm{R}\)), what is the correct order of reactivity of alkyl halides in both \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) and \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) nucleophilic substitution mechanisms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Role of the Leaving Group in Nucleophilic Substitution
Both \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) and \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) mechanisms involve cleavage of the carbon-halogen bond during the rate-determining transition state or intermediate formation.

Step 2: Factors Influencing Leaving Group Ability
Leaving group ability depends on carbon-halogen bond strength and the basicity/stability of the departing halide ion. Weaker bonds and weaker conjugate bases make superior leaving groups.

Step 3: Evaluation of Bond Strengths and Anion Stability
The \(\mathrm{C-I}\) bond is the weakest (\(234\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)) and iodide (\(\mathrm{I^-}\)) is the largest, most polarisable, and weakest base, departing most readily. Conversely, the \(\mathrm{C-F}\) bond is extremely strong (\(452\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)) and fluoride departs very poorly.

Step 4: Conclusion
The reactivity order in both substitution mechanisms is \(\mathrm{R-I > R-Br > R-Cl \gg R-F}\).

Final Answer:
\(\mathrm{R-I > R-Br > R-Cl \gg R-F}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q40 - Stereochemical outcome of bimolecular substitution hydrolysis

questiontext.text: When optically active \((-)\)-2-bromooctane is allowed to react with sodium hydroxide under conditions that favour an \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) mechanism, the stereochemical outcome of the formed octan-2-ol is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Reaction Conditions and Mechanism Identification
Reaction of 2-bromooctane with hydroxide ion under \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) conditions proceeds via backside attack of \(\mathrm{OH^-}\) on the secondary stereocentre.

Step 2: Backside Attack and Walden Inversion
The nucleophile approaches from the face exactly opposite to the departing bromide ion. As the \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond breaks, the other three groups attached to the stereocentre invert their spatial arrangement.

Step 3: Change in Optical Activity
Starting from the \((-)\)-enantiomer of 2-bromooctane, stereochemical inversion yields the \((+)\)-enantiomer of octan-2-ol, with the hydroxyl group occupying the position opposite to where the bromide had been.

Step 4: Conclusion
The product formed is \((+)\)-octan-2-ol with complete inversion of configuration.

Final Answer:
\((+)\)-Octan-2-ol with complete inversion of configuration

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q41 - Racemisation mechanism in unimolecular hydrolysis

questiontext.text: Hydrolysis of optically active 2-bromobutane under \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction conditions results in the formation of an optically inactive mixture, \((\pm)\)-butan-2-ol. Why does racemisation occur?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Formation of Intermediate in Step I
In the slow step of the \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction, the \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond breaks heterolytically to yield a sec-butyl carbocation (\(\mathrm{CH_3-\overset{+}{C}H-CH_2CH_3}\)).

Step 2: Geometry of the Carbocation
The carbocation carbon is \(sp^2\)-hybridised with a trigonal planar geometry and an unhybridised empty p-orbital perpendicular to the molecular plane; it is achiral.

Step 3: Dual-Face Nucleophilic Attack
The attacking nucleophile (\(\mathrm{OH^-}\) or \(\mathrm{H_2O}\)) can attack the empty p-orbital with equal probability from the front face (giving retention of configuration) or from the back face (giving inversion of configuration).

Step 4: Outcome of Equimolar Products
Attack from both sides in equal proportions produces an equimolar mixture of dextrorotatory and laevorotatory enantiomers, resulting in an optically inactive racemic modification (\((\pm)\)-butan-2-ol).

Step 5: Conclusion
Racemisation occurs because the intermediate carbocation is planar and achiral, permitting nucleophilic attack equally from either face.

Final Answer:
The intermediate carbocation is \(sp^2\)-hybridised, planar, and achiral, allowing nucleophilic attack with equal probability from either face

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q42 - Retention of configuration without stereocenter bond cleavage

questiontext.text: When \((-)\)-2-methylbutan-1-ol is heated with concentrated hydrochloric acid, \((+)\)-1-chloro-2-methylbutane is obtained. This reaction is classified as proceeding with retention of configuration because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the Stereocentre
In 2-methylbutan-1-ol, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-C^*H(CH_3)-CH_2OH}\), carbon-2 (\(\mathrm{C^*}\)) is the chiral stereocentre attached to \(\mathrm{-H}\), \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{-CH_2CH_3}\), and \(\mathrm{-CH_2OH}\).

Step 2: Locate the Bond Broken
During reaction with \(\mathrm{HCl}\), the bond broken is between carbon-1 and the hydroxyl group (\(\mathrm{C_1-OH}\)), replacing \(\mathrm{-OH}\) with \(\mathrm{-Cl}\) to give \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-C^*H(CH_3)-CH_2Cl}\).

Step 3: Definition of Retention of Configuration
Retention of configuration is defined as the preservation of the spatial arrangement of bonds to an asymmetric center during a reaction. Since no bond to the \(\mathrm{C^*}\) stereocentre was cleaved, the spatial orientation of groups around \(\mathrm{C^*}\) remains unchanged.

Step 4: Sign of Optical Rotation vs Configuration
A change in the sign of optical rotation (from \((-)\) to \((+)\)) does not imply inversion of configuration, because optical rotation depends on the electronic nature of substituents around the stereocentre.

Step 5: Conclusion
The reaction proceeds with retention of configuration because no bond attached to the stereocentre is broken.

Final Answer:
No bond directly attached to the asymmetric stereocentre is broken during the chemical transformation

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q43 - Zaitsev dehydrohalogenation of secondary haloalkanes

questiontext.text: When 2-bromopentane is heated with alcoholic potassium hydroxide, dehydrohalogenation (\(\beta\)-elimination) occurs. According to Zaitsev's (Saytzeff's) rule, the major alkene formed is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) Carbons
In 2-bromopentane, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-CH(Br)-CH_3}\), carbon-2 is the \(\alpha\)-carbon holding bromine. It has two adjacent \(\beta\)-carbons: carbon-1 (with 3 \(\beta\)-hydrogens) and carbon-3 (with 2 \(\beta\)-hydrogens).

Step 2: Possible Elimination Products
Elimination of \(\mathrm{H}\) from C1 yields pent-1-ene (\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-CH=CH_2}\)). Elimination of \(\mathrm{H}\) from C3 yields pent-2-ene (\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH=CH-CH_3}\)).

Step 3: Apply Zaitsev's Rule
Zaitsev's rule states that in dehydrohalogenation reactions, the preferred major product is the alkene that has the greater number of alkyl groups attached to the doubly bonded carbons (more substituted alkene).

Step 4: Alkene Substitution Comparison
Pent-2-ene is disubstituted (bears two alkyl groups: methyl and ethyl), whereas pent-1-ene is monosubstituted (bears one propyl group). Therefore, pent-2-ene is thermodynamically more stable and forms as the major product (81% vs 19%).

Step 5: Conclusion
The major product is pent-2-ene.

Final Answer:
Pent-2-ene

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q44 - Competition between substitution and elimination pathways

questiontext.text: In the competition between nucleophilic substitution and \(\beta\)-elimination for alkyl halides, which combination of substrate and reagent most strongly favours elimination over substitution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Fundamental Competition Concept
An alkyl halide containing \(\beta\)-hydrogens undergoes competition between nucleophile attack at carbon (substitution) and base abstraction of a proton (elimination).

Step 2: Steric Effects of the Substrate
In tertiary alkyl halides, the electrophilic carbon is surrounded by bulky alkyl groups that sterically prevent nucleophiles from approaching, disfavoring \(\mathrm{S_N2}\).

Step 3: Steric and Basicity Effects of the Reagent
A strong, sterically hindered (bulky) base, such as potassium tert-butoxide, encounters high steric hindrance when approaching carbon; instead, it readily abstracts an accessible proton from the less hindered \(\beta\)-position.

Step 4: Temperature Factor
Higher temperatures thermodynamically and kinetically favor elimination (entropy increases due to formation of more species).

Step 5: Conclusion
Elimination is maximized when a tertiary alkyl halide reacts with a strong, bulky base at elevated temperature.

Final Answer:
A tertiary alkyl halide reacting with a strong, bulky base at elevated temperature

A tertiary alkyl halide reacting with a strong, bulky base at elevated temperature

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q45 - Anhydrous conditions for Grignard reagent preparation

questiontext.text: Grignard reagents (\(\mathrm{RMgX}\)) must be prepared and preserved strictly under anhydrous conditions in dry ether because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Nature of Grignard Reagents
In an organomagnesium halide (\(\mathrm{R^{\delta-}-Mg^{\delta+}X}\)), the carbon-magnesium bond is covalent but highly polarized, imparting strong carbanionic character to the alkyl carbon.

Step 2: Reactivity with Proton Donors
Grignard reagents are powerful bases and strong nucleophiles. They react vigorously with any compound containing an active hydrogen (water, alcohols, amines, acids): \(\mathrm{RMgX + H_2O \rightarrow RH + Mg(OH)X}\).

Step 3: Consequence of Moisture Contamination
Even trace amounts of moisture destroy the reagent by protonating the carbanion to yield the corresponding hydrocarbon.

Step 4: Conclusion
Anhydrous conditions are essential because Grignard reagents react readily with proton donors like water to form hydrocarbons.

Final Answer:
The highly polar \(\mathrm{C-Mg}\) bond reacts rapidly with any proton donor, converting the Grignard reagent into a hydrocarbon

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q46 - Symmetrical alkane synthesis via Wurtz reaction

questiontext.text: When ethyl bromide (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Br}\)) is treated with metallic sodium in dry ether, the principal organic product obtained is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Principle of the Wurtz Reaction
Alkyl halides react with sodium metal in dry ether to yield symmetrical alkanes containing double the number of carbon atoms present in the starting halide.

Step 2: Chemical Equation
Two molecules of ethyl bromide couple in the presence of sodium: \(\mathrm{2CH_3CH_2Br + 2Na \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_3 + 2NaBr}\).

Step 3: Identify the Product
The coupled hydrocarbon is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3}\), which is n-butane.

Step 4: Conclusion
The product of the reaction is n-butane.

Final Answer:
n-Butane

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q47 - Resistance of haloarenes to nucleophilic substitution

questiontext.text: Aryl halides are extremely unreactive towards nucleophilic substitution reactions compared to alkyl halides. Which of the following is NOT a genuine reason for this low reactivity?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate Resonance Effect
In haloarenes, the lone pair of electrons on halogen is in conjugation with the aromatic \(\pi\)-system, imparting partial double-bond character to the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond and making it shorter and stronger than a single bond.

Step 2: Evaluate Carbon Hybridisation
The aromatic carbon is \(sp^2\)-hybridised (33% s-character), which is more electronegative and holds the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bonding electrons tighter (bond length \(169\,\mathrm{pm}\)) than the \(sp^3\) carbon in haloalkanes (bond length \(177\,\mathrm{pm}\)). Shorter bonds are stronger and harder to cleave.

Step 3: Evaluate Intermediate Stability and Repulsion
Heterolysis to form a phenyl cation does not occur because the phenyl cation cannot be resonance stabilised. Furthermore, repulsion exists between the electron-rich nucleophile and the aromatic \(\pi\)-electron cloud.

Step 4: Identify Incorrect Statement
The assertion that the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond in haloarenes is longer and weaker is factually false; it is actually shorter and stronger.

Step 5: Conclusion
The statement that the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond is longer and weaker is NOT a valid reason for low reactivity.

Final Answer:
The \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond in haloarenes is longer and weaker than the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond in haloalkanes

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q48 - Activating effect of nitro groups on haloarene substitution

questiontext.text: The presence of a nitro (\(\mathrm{-NO_2}\)) group at the ortho or para position of chlorobenzene dramatically increases its reactivity towards nucleophilic substitution by hydroxide ion, but a nitro group at the meta position shows virtually no activating effect. Why?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mechanism of Nucleophilic Aromatic Substitution
Nucleophilic substitution in haloarenes proceeds via addition of the nucleophile to form a resonance-stabilised carbanion (Meisenheimer intermediate), followed by departure of halide.

Step 2: Charge Distribution in the Intermediate
In the carbanionic intermediate, resonance structures show that the negative charge is delocalised exclusively onto the carbons located ortho and para to the position of nucleophilic attack.

Step 3: Stabilisation by Ortho and Para Nitro Groups
When an electron-withdrawing \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\) group is at an ortho or para position, it directly accommodates the negative charge via resonance, significantly lowering the activation energy.

Step 4: Absence of Effect at Meta Position
In meta-nitrochlorobenzene, none of the resonating structures of the carbanionic intermediate place the negative charge on the carbon bearing the \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\) group. Thus, the meta-nitro group cannot stabilise the carbanion by resonance.

Step 5: Conclusion
The effect occurs only at ortho and para positions because negative charge is delocalised onto those carbons and stabilized by the nitro group, but never onto the meta carbon.

Final Answer:
The carbanionic intermediate delocalises negative charge onto ortho and para positions where the \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\) group directly stabilises it, whereas negative charge never appears on the meta carbon

answer.text: A meta-nitro group donates electron density into the ring through resonance to deactivate nucleophilic attack
Ortho and para nitro groups generate a stable planar carbocation that accelerates substitution
The meta position causes severe steric hindrance that physically blocks attack of hydroxide ion

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q49 - Electronic dualism of halogens in aromatic substitution

questiontext.text: Although chlorine is an electron-withdrawing group, it directs incoming electrophiles to the ortho and para positions during electrophilic aromatic substitution of chlorobenzene. How are these opposing characteristics rationalised?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Dual Electronic Nature of Halogens
A halogen attached to a benzene ring exerts an electron-withdrawing inductive effect (\(\mathrm{-I}\)) and an electron-donating resonance effect (\(\mathrm{+M}\)) via its lone pair of electrons.

Step 2: Origin of Deactivation
Because chlorine is strongly electronegative, its inductive withdrawal (\(\mathrm{-I}\)) is stronger than its resonance donation (\(\mathrm{+M}\)). This results in a net withdrawal of electron density from the ring, destabilising the arenium carbocation intermediate and deactivating the ring compared to benzene.

Step 3: Origin of Ortho/Para Orientation
During electrophilic attack at ortho and para positions, an additional resonance structure is possible where the lone pair on chlorine directly delocalises into the ring, placing a positive charge on chlorine (complete octet). This resonance stabilisation is absent during meta attack.

Step 4: Balancing Reactivity and Orientation
Reactivity is governed by the stronger inductive effect (net deactivation), while orientation is controlled by the resonance effect (favouring ortho and para attack).

Step 5: Conclusion
Reactivity is controlled by inductive electron withdrawal, while orientation is directed to ortho and para by resonance stabilization.

Final Answer:
Inductive electron withdrawal (\(\mathrm{-I}\)) deactivates the ring and controls overall reactivity, while resonance electron donation (\(\mathrm{+M}\)) stabilises carbocation intermediates specifically for ortho and para attack

answer.text: Inductive electron withdrawal (\(\mathrm{-I}\)) deactivates the ring and controls overall reactivity, while resonance electron donation (\(\mathrm{+M}\)) stabilises carbocation intermediates specifically for ortho and para attack
Resonance withdrawal (\(\mathrm{-M}\)) deactivates the ring, while inductive donation (\(\mathrm{+I}\)) directs the incoming electrophile

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q50 - Cross coupling versus homocoupling in haloarene reactions

questiontext.text: What are the primary organic products of the Wurtz-Fittig reaction and the Fittig reaction, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of the Wurtz-Fittig Reaction
When a mixture of an alkyl halide and an aryl halide is treated with sodium metal in dry ether, coupling occurs between the alkyl group and the aryl group: \(\mathrm{Ar-X + 2Na + R-X \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} Ar-R + 2NaX}\). The product is an alkylarene (such as toluene from bromobenzene and bromomethane).

Step 2: Definition of the Fittig Reaction
When aryl halides alone are treated with sodium in dry ether, homocoupling between two aryl groups takes place: \(\mathrm{2Ar-X + 2Na \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} Ar-Ar + 2NaX}\). The product is a biaryl (diphenyl / biphenyl).

Step 3: Comparison and Distinction
The Wurtz-Fittig reaction is a cross-coupling yielding alkylarenes, whereas the Fittig reaction is a homocoupling yielding diphenyl derivatives.

Step 4: Conclusion
The Wurtz-Fittig gives an alkylarene, and the Fittig gives a diphenyl.

Final Answer:
An alkylarene from an alkyl halide and aryl halide; a diphenyl (biaryl) from two aryl halides

An alkylarene from an alkyl halide and aryl halide; a diphenyl (biaryl) from two aryl halides
An alkane from an alkyl halide and aryl halide; an alkylarene from two aryl halides
A symmetrical dialkyl ether; an aromatic aldehyde

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q51 - Photochemical oxidation of chloroform to phosgene

questiontext.text: Chloroform (\(\mathrm{CHCl_3}\)) is stored in closed, dark amber-coloured bottles filled completely to the top because in the presence of light and air it slowly oxidises to form:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Oxidation Pathway of Chloroform
Chloroform reacts slowly with atmospheric oxygen when exposed to light through a free radical autoxidation process.

Step 2: Chemical Reaction Equation
The balanced oxidation reaction is: \(\mathrm{2CHCl_3 + O_2 \xrightarrow{light} 2COCl_2 + 2HCl}\).

Step 3: Toxicity of By-product
The product \(\mathrm{COCl_2}\) is carbonyl chloride, commonly known as phosgene, which is an extremely lethal and toxic gas historically used in chemical warfare.

Step 4: Storage Precaution Rationale
Completely filling dark bottles excludes atmospheric oxygen and blocks light, preventing the formation of toxic phosgene.

Step 5: Conclusion
Chloroform oxidises in light and air to form carbonyl chloride (phosgene).

Final Answer:
Carbonyl chloride (Phosgene, \(\mathrm{COCl_2}\)), an extremely poisonous gas

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q52 - Ozone depletion and bioaccumulation of polyhalogen compounds

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements correctly pairs Freon-12 (\(\mathrm{CCl_2F_2}\)) and \(\mathrm{p,p'\text{-}DDT}\) with their principal environmental hazards, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Environmental Hazard of Freons
Freon-12 (\(\mathrm{CCl_2F_2}\)) is extremely stable in the lower atmosphere, diffusing unchanged into the stratosphere where ultraviolet radiation cleaves carbon-chlorine bonds to generate chlorine free radicals that catalytically deplete the protective ozone layer.

Step 2: Environmental Hazard of DDT
\(\mathrm{p,p'}\)-Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) is chemically persistent and fat-soluble. Animals and humans metabolise it very slowly, causing it to accumulate in fatty tissues along food chains (biomagnification) and showing high toxicity towards fish and predatory birds.

Step 3: Matching Pairs Check
Freon-12 is responsible for stratospheric ozone depletion, and DDT causes persistence and bioaccumulation in fatty tissues.

Step 4: Conclusion
Freon-12 depletes the stratospheric ozone layer, while DDT bioaccumulates in fatty tissues.

Final Answer:

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS12_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_STATEMENT_Q01 - Hybridisation of carbon bonded to halogen

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In haloalkanes, the halogen atom is attached to an \(sp^3\) hybridised carbon atom of an alkyl group.

Statement II: In haloarenes, the halogen atom is attached to an \(sp^2\) hybridised carbon atom of an aryl group.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Organic halogen compounds are classified into haloalkanes and haloarenes based on the state of hybridisation of the carbon atom to which the halogen atom is directly bonded.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion on Haloalkanes
In aliphatic halogen derivatives (haloalkanes or alkyl halides), the halogen atom is covalently bonded to an \(sp^3\) hybridised tetrahedral carbon atom of an aliphatic carbon chain (such as in ethyl chloride, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Cl}\)). Hence, this assertion accurately reflects the structural definition.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Assertion on Haloarenes
In aromatic halogen derivatives (haloarenes or aryl halides), the halogen atom is bonded directly to a planar, aromatic ring carbon atom possessing \(sp^2\) hybridisation (such as in chlorobenzene, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5Cl}\)). Hence, this assertion is also completely valid.

Step 4: Comparison and Synthesis
Both assertions accurately define the hybridisation states of the carbon atoms bearing the halogen atom in haloalkanes and haloarenes, respectively.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Both the statement regarding haloalkanes and the statement regarding haloarenes are scientifically correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS12_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_STATEMENT_Q02 - Definitions of geminal and vicinal dihalides

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Dihaloalkanes having both halogen atoms bonded to the same carbon atom are designated as geminal dihalides.

Statement II: Dihaloalkanes having halogen atoms bonded to two adjacent carbon atoms are designated as vicinal dihalides.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Dihaloalkanes are classified on the basis of the relative positions of the two halogen atoms along the carbon framework.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion on Geminal Dihalides
When two identical halogen atoms are bonded to the very same carbon atom of the alkyl chain, they are termed geminal dihalides (or alkylidene halides, such as \(\mathrm{CH_3CHX_2}\)). Therefore, this description of geminal halides is precise and correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Assertion on Vicinal Dihalides
When two halogen atoms are bonded to adjacent (neighbouring) carbon atoms of the hydrocarbon chain, they are termed vicinal dihalides (or alkylene dihalides, such as \(\mathrm{CH_2X-CH_2X}\)). Thus, this description of vicinal halides is also fully accurate.

Step 4: Comparison and Synthesis
Both definitions correctly state the structural distinction between geminal and vicinal dihalides.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Both the statement regarding geminal dihalides and the statement regarding vicinal dihalides are scientifically correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS12_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_STATEMENT_Q03 - Role of dry acetone in Finkelstein reaction

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Alkyl iodides are often prepared by the reaction of alkyl chlorides or bromides with sodium iodide in dry acetone.

Statement II: The precipitation of sodium chloride or sodium bromide in dry acetone drives the halogen exchange reaction forward according to Le Chatelier's principle.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Finkelstein reaction involves nucleophilic halogen exchange to synthesise alkyl iodides from alkyl chlorides or bromides using sodium iodide dissolved in an appropriate solvent.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Synthetic Method
Alkyl iodides are typically synthesised by reacting alkyl chlorides or bromides with \(\mathrm{NaI}\) dissolved in dry acetone (\(\mathrm{R-X + NaI \rightarrow R-I + NaX}\), where \(\mathrm{X = Cl, Br}\)). This matches the reaction conditions of the Finkelstein halogen exchange. Thus, this assertion is scientifically valid.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reaction Driving Force
Sodium iodide (\(\mathrm{NaI}\)) is soluble in dry acetone due to covalent character, whereas the resulting sodium chloride (\(\mathrm{NaCl}\)) and sodium bromide (\(\mathrm{NaBr}\)) are predominantly ionic and insoluble in acetone, precipitating out of solution. By Le Chatelier's principle, continuous removal of the solid halide salt shifts the dynamic equilibrium toward the product side, driving the halogen exchange reaction forward to completion. Thus, this explanatory assertion is accurate.

Step 4: Comparison and Synthesis
Both the stated synthetic method and the thermodynamic rationale for the forward drive in acetone are correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Both the statement regarding the synthesis of alkyl iodides and the statement regarding the precipitation of sodium salts in dry acetone are scientifically correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS12_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_STATEMENT_Q04 - Effect of branching on boiling points of haloalkanes

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The boiling points of isomeric haloalkanes increase with an increase in carbon chain branching.

Statement II: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane has a lower boiling point than 1-bromobutane.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Intermolecular van der Waals forces depend directly on the surface area of contact between organic molecules. For isomeric haloalkanes having the same molecular mass, branching leads to a more spherical and compact shape.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Branching Trend
With increased branching, the molecular surface area decreases, leading to weaker van der Waals attractions and consequently a lower boiling point. Thus, the boiling point of isomeric haloalkanes decreases (rather than increases) with branching. Hence, the general claim regarding branching increasing the boiling point is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Specific Isomeric Comparison
Comparing the isomers 1-bromobutane (straight-chain, normal boiling point \(375\ \mathrm{K}\)) and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tertiary branched, boiling point \(346\ \mathrm{K}\)), the branched isomer has a smaller surface area and thus a lower boiling point. Hence, the comparison between these two butyl bromide isomers is scientifically valid.

Step 4: Comparison and Synthesis
The general assertion asserting an increase in boiling point with branching is incorrect, while the specific comparison indicating a lower boiling point for 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The statement claiming that branching increases the boiling point of haloalkanes is incorrect, whereas the statement indicating that 2-bromo-2-methylpropane boils at a lower temperature than 1-bromobutane is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS12_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_STATEMENT_Q05 - Optical rotation properties of enantiomeric pairs

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Optical isomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other are called enantiomers.

Statement II: Enantiomers possess identical optical rotation in terms of both magnitude and direction.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Stereoisomers related to each other as non-superimposable mirror images are known as enantiomers. Enantiomers possess identical physical properties such as melting point, boiling point, and density, but differ in their interaction with plane-polarised light.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Definition of Enantiomers
By definition, stereoisomers that cannot be superimposed on their mirror images are designated as enantiomers. Hence, this definition is entirely accurate.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Optical Rotation Behaviour
Enantiomers rotate the plane of plane-polarised light by equal magnitude but in opposite directions: one isomer rotates the plane to the right (dextrorotatory, \(+\)) while the other rotates it to the left by the identical angle (laevorotatory, \(-\)). Claiming that their rotation is in the same direction is scientifically false.

Step 4: Comparison and Synthesis
The definition of enantiomers is correct, but the claim regarding the identical direction of optical rotation is incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The statement defining enantiomers as non-superimposable mirror images is correct, whereas the statement asserting that they rotate plane-polarised light in the same direction is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS12_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_STATEMENT_Q06 - Stereochemical outcomes of SN2 and SN1 reactions

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_N2}\)) of an optically active haloalkane proceeds with complete retention of configuration.

Statement II: Unimolecular nucleophilic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_N1}\)) of an optically active haloalkane proceeds with complete inversion of configuration without any racemisation.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nucleophilic substitution mechanisms exhibit distinct stereochemical pathways depending on whether substitution occurs via a concerted transition state (\(\mathrm{S_N2}\)) or via an intermediate planar carbocation (\(\mathrm{S_N1}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation of the Bimolecular Substitution Pathway
In the \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) mechanism, the nucleophile attacks from the side directly opposite to the leaving group (backside attack), leading to complete inversion of configuration (Walden inversion), not retention. Hence, the assertion claiming retention of configuration for bimolecular substitution is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Unimolecular Substitution Pathway
In the \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) mechanism, the reaction proceeds via an \(sp^2\) hybridised planar carbocation intermediate. Attack of the nucleophile can occur with almost equal probability from either face of the flat carbocation, resulting in racemisation (yielding an equimolar or near-equimolar mixture of enantiomers), rather than complete inversion without racemisation. Hence, the assertion regarding unimolecular substitution is incorrect.

Step 4: Comparison and Synthesis
Both mechanisms have been attributed the wrong stereochemical outcomes: bimolecular substitution yields inversion rather than retention, and unimolecular substitution yields racemisation rather than complete inversion without racemisation.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Both the statement asserting retention for bimolecular substitution and the statement asserting complete inversion without racemisation for unimolecular substitution are incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS12_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_STATEMENT_Q07 - Reactivity and bond length in chlorobenzene versus chloroethane

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Chlorobenzene undergoes nucleophilic substitution reactions under much milder conditions than chloroethane.

Statement II: The \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond length in chlorobenzene is shorter (\(169\ \mathrm{pm}\)) than that in chloroethane (\(177\ \mathrm{pm}\)) due to resonance and \(sp^2\) hybridisation of carbon.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Aryl halides are extremely less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution compared to alkyl halides due to resonance effects, difference in hybridisation of the carbon atom in the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond, instability of phenyl cation, and possible repulsion between incoming nucleophile and electron-rich arene ring.

Step 2: Evaluation of Nucleophilic Substitution Reactivity
Haloarenes like chlorobenzene are extremely unreactive towards nucleophilic substitution and require harsh conditions (such as \(623\ \mathrm{K}\) and \(300\ \mathrm{atm}\) in the Dow process for replacement of chlorine by a hydroxyl group), whereas haloalkanes like chloroethane undergo nucleophilic substitution readily under mild aqueous alkaline heating. Therefore, asserting that chlorobenzene reacts under much milder conditions is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of Carbon-Halogen Bond Characteristics
In chlorobenzene, the lone pair on chlorine enters into resonance with the benzene ring, imparting partial double-bond character to the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond. Furthermore, the carbon atom is \(sp^2\) hybridised (greater \(s\)-character, holding electrons more tightly) compared to \(sp^3\) hybridised carbon in chloroethane. Consequently, the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond length in chlorobenzene is \(169\ \mathrm{pm}\), which is significantly shorter than the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond length in chloroethane (\(177\ \mathrm{pm}\)). Hence, this assertion is scientifically valid.

Step 4: Comparison and Synthesis
The assertion regarding the relative ease of nucleophilic substitution in chlorobenzene is false, while the structural observation regarding bond length and resonance stabilization is true.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The statement proposing that chlorobenzene undergoes nucleophilic substitution under milder conditions than chloroethane is incorrect, whereas the statement describing the shorter carbon-chlorine bond length in chlorobenzene due to resonance and hybridisation is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS12_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_STATEMENT_Q08 - Regioselectivity and Saytzeff rule in dehydrohalogenation

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Alexander Zaitsev's rule states that in dehydrohalogenation reactions, the preferred alkene is the one having fewer alkyl groups attached to the doubly bonded carbon atoms.

Statement II: Dehydrohalogenation of 2-bromopentane with alcoholic potassium hydroxide produces pent-1-ene as the major product.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In \(\beta\)-elimination (dehydrohalogenation) of secondary and tertiary alkyl halides that can yield more than one alkene, regioselectivity is governed by Zaitsev's (Saytzeff's) rule.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Stated Elimination Rule
Zaitsev's rule explicitly states that in dehydrohalogenation reactions, the preferred product is that alkene which has the greater number of alkyl groups attached to the doubly bonded carbon atoms (the more substituted, more stable alkene). Thus, asserting that it produces the alkene with fewer alkyl groups is false.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Dehydrohalogenation of 2-Bromopentane
When 2-bromopentane is heated with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\), elimination can yield pent-2-ene (disubstituted alkene) or pent-1-ene (monosubstituted alkene). In accordance with Zaitsev's rule, the more substituted alkene, pent-2-ene, is the major product (\(81\%\)), whereas pent-1-ene is the minor product (\(19\%\)). Claiming that pent-1-ene is the major product is scientifically false.

Step 4: Comparison and Synthesis
Both assertions contradict established chemical principles: the first incorrectly states the definition of Zaitsev's rule, and the second wrongly designates the less-substituted alkene as the major elimination product.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Both the statement regarding the preference for less-substituted alkenes in Zaitsev elimination and the statement identifying pent-1-ene as the major product are incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS12_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_STATEMENT3_Q01 - Structural classification of allylic vinylic and benzylic halides

questiontext.text:
Given below are three statements:

Statement I: Allylic halides are compounds in which the halogen atom is bonded to an \(sp^3\) hybridised carbon atom adjacent to a carbon-carbon double bond.

Statement II: Vinylic halides are compounds in which the halogen atom is bonded directly to an \(sp^2\) hybridised carbon atom of a carbon-carbon double bond.

Statement III: Benzylic halides are compounds in which the halogen atom is bonded directly to an \(sp^2\) hybridised aromatic ring carbon atom.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Halogenated organic compounds are classified according to the hybridisation and positional environment of the carbon atom bearing the halogen atom.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion on Allylic Halides
In allylic halides, the halogen atom is attached to an \(sp^3\) hybridised carbon atom directly adjacent to a carbon-carbon double bond (\(\mathrm{-C=C-C(X)-}\)). Hence, the description of allylic halides is scientifically accurate.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Assertion on Vinylic Halides
In vinylic halides, the halogen atom is attached directly to an \(sp^2\) hybridised carbon atom forming part of an aliphatic carbon-carbon double bond (\(\mathrm{-C=C(X)-}\)). Hence, the description of vinylic halides is scientifically accurate.

Step 4: Evaluation of the Assertion on Benzylic Halides
In benzylic halides, the halogen atom is attached to an \(sp^3\) hybridised carbon atom that is directly attached to an aromatic ring (such as benzyl chloride, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2Cl}\)). Compounds where halogen is attached directly to an \(sp^2\) ring carbon atom are aryl halides, not benzylic halides. Hence, the description given for benzylic halides is incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The assertion defining allylic halides and the assertion defining vinylic halides are both correct, whereas the assertion describing benzylic halides is incorrect. Therefore, the assertions regarding allylic and vinylic halides alone are correct.

answer.text: Statement I and Statement II only are correct.
Statement II and Statement III only are correct.
Statement I and Statement III only are correct.
